name: Follicular unit transplantation (FUT)

card.summary: Strip-harvest hair transplant: a scalp strip is removed and dissected into grafts, leaving a thin linear donor scar.
card.aka: FUT, strip harvesting, strip surgery, FUSS
card.note: Leaves a linear donor scar, which is the main reason many patients choose FUE instead.

quick.overview:
Follicular unit transplantation removes a thin strip of hair-bearing skin from the back of the scalp, which technicians dissect under microscopes into natural follicular units for implanting in balding areas.

It became the standard hair transplant approach in the 1990s and is often compared with follicular unit extraction (FUE), which avoids a strip incision.
quick.mechanism: Grafts from the donor zone retain resistance to pattern hair loss, so transplanted hairs are described as lasting. The strip method allows many grafts from a single session, with the wound closed by sutures.
quick.risks: The donor site retains a thin linear scar that is usually concealed by surrounding hair. Recovery includes stitches or staples and about two weeks of healing; shock loss and other graft-related effects are described.

lead: Follicular unit transplantation (FUT), also called strip harvesting, is a hair transplant technique in which a strip of scalp is taken from the donor region and divided under stereo-microscopes into follicular units for implantation [1][2]. Wikipedia describes strip excision as replacing plug grafts in the 1980s, with microscopic dissection of strips developed in the late 1980s [1].

The procedure leaves a thin linear scar that is typically hidden by hair; a 2002 paper introducing FUE described donor scarring after strip excision as infrequent but concerning enough to warrant an alternative [2].

paras: Wikipedia gives a typical strip size of about 1 to 1.5 cm by 15 to 30 cm, with assistants dissecting follicular units and the donor wound closed, sometimes with a trichophytic closure said to produce a finer scar [1]. Recovery is described as about two weeks, with removal of sutures unless they are dissolvable [1].

Wikipedia describes Carlos Uebel and William Rassman popularising many small grafts in the 1980s, and B. L. Limmer using stereo-microscopes to split strips into micrografts in the late 1980s [1]. Walter Unger described the safe donor zone in 1994 [1].
Wikipedia says FUE leaves scattered small scars rather than a linear scar, but involves longer surgery, higher cost and, according to some surgeons, a lower proportion of successful follicles [1].
No studies found. The 2002 paper that introduced FUE discusses FUT donor scarring as its motivation [2].

timeline.event: Walter Unger defines the safe donor zone [1].
FUE introduced as an alternative to strip harvesting [2].
